purpose: Independent smoke-test evaluation of Phase 4 Lesson Reconciliation quality. No prior scores are included.

lesson.title: Biblioteca de manipulação de texto: NLTK e Spacy
lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é consolidar as técnicas apresentadas de processamento de textos nos encontros anteriores utilizando as bibliotecas NLTK e Spacy. O objetivo desta aplicação é permitir que a pessoa desenvolvedora consiga compreender como as ferramentas de mercado são utilizadas na implementação de técnicas de processamento de linguagem natural.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Loading pre-defined Portuguese texts with NLTK
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using NLTK's examples module to load Portuguese literary texts and newspaper corpora for linguistic analysis.
coverage_criteria: Student can import the Portuguese examples module and list the available text objects (e.g., ptext1, ptext2) with their descriptions.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly shows the import and setup of Portuguese texts and how to view them.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Loading data is a fundamental first step; this candidate focuses solely on the loading process, which is small enough for one to three focused questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Generating a concordance for a word
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using the concordance() method to display a word in its surrounding context within a text.
coverage_criteria: Student can call the concordance method on a text object and interpret the output showing the word in context.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides a direct example with ptext1.concordance('olhos') and explains its use.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concordance generation is a single, well-defined operation that can be tested with a specific word.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Finding words with similar contextual distribution
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using the similar() method to identify words that appear in similar contexts based on their distribution in the text.
coverage_criteria: Student can use similar() on a text object and list words that share similar contexts.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates similar() on ptext1 and ptext3 with example outputs.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific, checkable function call that can be verified with a single question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Extracting significant collocations from text
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using the collocations() method to find statistically significant word pairs or phrases.
coverage_criteria: Student can call collocations() on a text and identify common multi-word expressions.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows collocations() output for ptext1, listing phrases like 'Quincas Borba' and 'Lobo Neves'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a discrete, checkable operation that requires understanding the output of one method.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Searching text with regular expressions
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using the findall() method with regex patterns to extract words or phrases matching a pattern.
coverage_criteria: Student can construct a regex pattern and apply findall() to retrieve matching strings from a text.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates findall() with a regex pattern to capture words after 'olhos'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific technique combining regex with NLTK's search, testable with a short exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Generating random text based on a source text
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using the generate() method to produce random sentences that mimic the style of the training text.
coverage_criteria: Student can invoke generate() on a text object and explain that the output is based on the text's statistical model.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows generate() on ptext3 with a sample output.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a simple, self-contained feature that can be assessed with a single question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Tokenizing text into words and punctuation
before_phase4_candidates.description: Understanding that NLTK represents text as a list of tokens (words and punctuation) that have been segmented.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that a sentence like psent1 is a list of string tokens and can inspect its length.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly shows psent1 as a tokenized list and discusses its length and individual tokens.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Tokenization is a core concept; this candidate isolates the recognition of tokenized form, which is small enough for a couple of questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Extracting the unique vocabulary of a text
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using Python's set and sorted to obtain the distinct words in a tokenized text.
coverage_criteria: Student can apply set() to a tokenized list to get unique words and sort them.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows sorted(set(psent1)) to get the vocabulary.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a simple one-liner that can be verified by asking for the vocabulary of a short list.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using list comprehensions to filter and transform text
before_phase4_candidates.description: Applying Python list comprehensions to perform operations like case conversion, filtering by endings, or length constraints on tokens.
coverage_criteria: Student can write a list comprehension that converts tokens to uppercase or filters tokens longer than a given length.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides several list comprehension examples on tokens, such as [w.upper() for w in psent2].
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: List comprehensions are a versatile tool; this candidate focuses on their application to text processing, which is a specific, testable skill.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Computing word frequency distributions
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using FreqDist to count word occurrences, find the most common word, and sample frequent words.
coverage_criteria: Student can create a FreqDist from a text, query the count of a specific word, and retrieve the most frequent tokens.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates FreqDist with ptext1, showing fd1['olhos'] and fd1.max().
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Frequency distribution is a fundamental NLP operation; this candidate covers the basic API calls, which can be assessed with a few questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Accessing the Machado de Assis corpus in NLTK
before_phase4_candidates.description: Loading the complete works of Machado de Assis from nltk.corpus.machado, inspecting file IDs, and retrieving raw text or word lists.
coverage_criteria: Student can import the machado corpus, list its file IDs, and access the words or raw text of a specific work.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows how to load the machado corpus, list fileids(), and access words and raw text.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a step-by-step corpus access procedure, testable with a handful of commands.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Extracting n-grams containing a specific word
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using ngrams() and FreqDist to find the most common sequences (e.g., 5-grams) that include a target word.
coverage_criteria: Student can generate 5-grams from a text and filter those containing a given word, then display the most frequent ones.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides a program that finds most common ngrams containing a target word, using ngrams and FreqDist.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This candidate focuses on a specific ngram extraction pattern, which can be tested with a different target word.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Accessing the MacMorpho POS-tagged corpus
before_phase4_candidates.description: Loading the MAC-MORPHO corpus, which contains Brazilian Portuguese news text with part-of-speech tags, and retrieving words, sentences, or tagged words.
coverage_criteria: Student can import mac_morpho, access its words, sents, and tagged_words, and distinguish between simple words and tagged tokens.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly shows how to access mac_morpho and its different representations.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a well-defined corpus access task, suitable for a practical exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Accessing the Floresta treebank and simplifying its tags
before_phase4_candidates.description: Loading the Floresta corpus, retrieving words and tagged words, and simplifying its complex tags (e.g., 'H+n' to 'n').
coverage_criteria: Student can import floresta, list its words and tagged words, and write a function to strip the syntactic portion of a tag.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows loading floresta, accessing tagged words, and creating simplify_tag to extract the POS part.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This task combines corpus access and a simple string manipulation, which is a focused, testable skill.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using the Floresta treebank's parsed sentences
before_phase4_candidates.description: Accessing parsed_sents() from the Floresta corpus to obtain syntactic trees (nested structures), which can be visualized or traversed.
coverage_criteria: Student can retrieve parsed sentences and explain that they represent syntactic structure, and optionally draw a tree.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source shows floresta.parsed_sents() and mentions the draw() method for visualization.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific feature of the treebank; understanding parsed outputs is a small, checkable concept.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Understanding ISO 8859-1 encoding for Portuguese text
before_phase4_candidates.description: Awareness that Portuguese text often uses ISO 8859-1 encoding in NLTK resources, and how to decode such text in Python.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the need for specifying encoding when opening Portuguese text files and can decode bytes using ISO 8859-1.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides an example of reading a file with 'ISO 8859-1' decoding and discusses the encoding.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Encoding is a practical detail; this candidate focuses on a single encoding standard, which is testable with a short explanation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Implementing a basic concordance function
before_phase4_candidates.description: Writing a function that searches for a word in a list of sentences and prints it with surrounding context, mimicking NLTK's concordance.
coverage_criteria: Student can define a function that takes a word and context width, iterates over sentences, and prints formatted concordance lines.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides a complete concordance() function in the Processing Tasks section.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a self-contained coding task that encapsulates indexing and formatting, suitable for a practical assessment.

before_phase4_candidates.label: NLTK word_tokenize for better tokenization
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using nltk.word_tokenize splits text into tokens while properly handling contractions like 'wasn't' into 'was' and "n't", unlike regex-based splitting.
coverage_criteria: Can explain why nltk.word_tokenize is better than simple regex splitting for handling English contractions.
Can demonstrate using nltk.word_tokenize on a sentence with contractions.
Can identify that 'was' and 'not' become separate tokens, useful for negation handling.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly demonstrates tokenization using both regex and NLTK's word_tokenize, highlighting the advantage of better handling contractions like 'wasn't'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Tokenization is a single step in NLP pipeline, and this candidate isolates the specific feature of handling contractions—small enough for focused assessment.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Porter Stemmer algorithm
before_phase4_candidates.description: Porter Stemmer is a rule-based stemming algorithm that reduces words to their stems by applying a series of suffix stripping rules.
coverage_criteria: Can describe the basic operation of Porter Stemmer as rule-based stemming.
Can use PorterStemmer from nltk.stem to stem a list of words.
Can identify that stemmed outputs may not be real words (e.g., 'generously' -> 'gener').

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates initializing PorterStemmer, applying it to plural words, and showing the stemmed outputs, explaining the rule-based approach.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Porter Stemmer is one specific stemming algorithm; understanding its behavior is a focused concept suitable for assessment.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Snowball Stemmer for multilingual stemming
before_phase4_candidates.description: Snowball Stemmer is a stemming algorithm that supports multiple languages and often produces more accurate stems than Porter Stemmer, as shown by stemming 'generously' to 'generous' vs 'gener'.
coverage_criteria: Can list several languages supported by SnowballStemmer.
Can initialize SnowballStemmer with a language and stem a word.
Can explain why Snowball Stemmer might be preferred over Porter Stemmer.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates SnowballStemmer, its language support, and compares its output with Porter Stemmer on 'generously'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Snowball Stemmer is a distinct tool with multilingual capability, a focused concept within stemming.

before_phase4_candidates.label: WordNet Lemmatizer for dictionary-based lemmatization
before_phase4_candidates.description: WordNetLemmatizer reduces words to their base dictionary form (lemma) using the WordNet lexical database. It requires NLTK data download (wordnet corpora). Unlike stemming, lemmas are actual words (e.g., 'flies' -> 'fly').
coverage_criteria: Can explain the difference between lemmatization and stemming.
Can instantiate WordNetLemmatizer and lemmatize a word.
Can identify that lemmatization depends on a lexical database like WordNet.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates lemmatization using WordNetLemmatizer, shows outputs on plural words, and contrasts with stemming implicitly.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Lemmatization is a key NLP normalization technique; this candidate captures its NLTK implementation and prerequisites, suitable for assessment.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Initializing a spaCy pipeline and processing text into a Doc
before_phase4_candidates.description: Use spacy.blank to create a language-specific pipeline and call it with a string to obtain a Doc object.
coverage_criteria: Write code to create a blank Portuguese pipeline 'nlp', process the string 'Olá mundo', and confirm the result is a Doc.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Sections 2 and 3 guide the student through creating blank pipelines for multiple languages and processing text, demonstrating the fundamental workflow.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single, atomic operation that is the prerequisite for all further spaCy processing.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Tokens and spans in spaCy
before_phase4_candidates.description: A Doc is a sequence of Token objects; a Span is a slice of the Doc. Access tokens by index.
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc for 'três cachorros e dois gatos', write code to retrieve the first token and create a span for 'três cachorros'.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 3 explicitly teaches the Doc, Token, and Span concepts through exercises.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the basic data structures is foundational and can be checked by asking for specific token and span retrieval.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Lexical attributes for pattern detection
before_phase4_candidates.description: Token attributes like `like_num` can identify numeric tokens. Combine attributes to find patterns like percentages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to find tokens that represent numbers in a Doc using `like_num`. Write a loop to detect a number followed by a '%' sign.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 4 uses `like_num` and `token.i+1` to find percentages, teaching how to use lexical attributes.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a specific, actionable technique for identifying patterns, not a broad overview.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Loading pre-trained NLP pipelines
before_phase4_candidates.description: Use `spacy.load` to load a trained pipeline (e.g., `pt_core_news_sm`) that can predict linguistic annotations.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load the Portuguese small pipeline and process a text, then print the Doc's text.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 7 demonstrates loading the Portuguese pipeline with `spacy.load`.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single step that enables access to pre-trained models, a key functionality of spaCy.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Components of a trained pipeline package
before_phase4_candidates.description: Trained pipelines include config.cfg (language and settings), binary weights for predictions, and strings.json (vocabulary mapping), but do not include the original training data.
coverage_criteria: List what is included in a spaCy pipeline package and explain why training data is not needed for predictions.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 6 explains that training data is NOT included and describes config, weights, and strings.json.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific factual knowledge point about pipeline packaging, suitable for a short comprehension check.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Predicting part-of-speech tags and dependencies
before_phase4_candidates.description: After processing text with a trained pipeline, each token has a .pos_ (coarse POS tag) and .dep_ (dependency label).
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc from a Portuguese pipeline, write a loop to print each token's text, .pos_, and .dep_.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 8, Part 1 has the student iterate tokens and print .pos_ and .dep_.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This focuses on two specific annotation types that are commonly used together.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Predicting named entities
before_phase4_candidates.description: Trained pipelines can identify named entities in a Doc. Access them via doc.ents and get their text and label (.label_).
coverage_criteria: Write code to iterate over doc.ents and print entity text and label. Use spacy.explain to describe a label.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 8, Part 2 and Section 9 demonstrate iterating entities and handling missed entities.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Named entity recognition is a distinct NLP task that can be practiced independently.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Manual correction of model predictions
before_phase4_candidates.description: When a trained model fails to recognize an entity, you can manually create a Span for the missed tokens.
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc where 'iPhone X' is not recognized, write code to create a Span for those two tokens.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 9 explicitly instructs the student to create a span for 'iPhone X' when the model misses it.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This teaches a practical workaround and emphasizes that models are not perfect, which is a valuable lesson.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Rule-based matching with Matcher
before_phase4_candidates.description: The Matcher class allows finding token sequences based on patterns defined with token attributes and operators.
coverage_criteria: Write code to initialize a Matcher, add a pattern that matches 'iPhone X', apply it to a Doc, and print the matched spans.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 11 walks through creating a Matcher, adding a pattern, and retrieving matches for 'iPhone X'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a focused tool for rule-based matching, distinct from statistical predictions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Writing complex match patterns
before_phase4_candidates.description: Patterns can use lemmas (LEMMA), POS tags, and quantifiers (e.g., '+', '*', '?') to match flexible sequences.
coverage_criteria: Write a pattern that matches a verb lemma 'baixar' followed by a proper noun, and a pattern for an adjective followed by one or two nouns.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Section 12 provides three exercises requiring patterns with lemmas, POS, and operators.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This advances from simple literal matching to linguistic-aware patterns, a key skill for information extraction.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Processamento de Linguagem Natural (PLN) – conceito e desafios
before_phase4_candidates.description: PLN é a área que estuda como fazer computadores entenderem línguas naturais. Por ser um problema não computável, as soluções são baseadas em aproximações estatísticas, resultando em incertezas e falsos positivos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar que PLN trata da compreensão de linguagem natural por máquinas.
Mencionar que as abordagens são estatísticas e aproximadas.
Dar exemplos de aplicações como extração de informações de documentos ou chatbots.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo dedica os primeiros minutos a definir PLN, contrastar com a leitura humana e destacar os desafios (aproximação estatística).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Conceito fundamental para contextualizar todo o restante do processamento de texto; um aluno precisa entender o propósito e limitações antes de usar ferramentas.

before_phase4_candidates.label: spaCy – biblioteca de PLN pronta para produção
before_phase4_candidates.description: spaCy é uma biblioteca open-source (MIT) para PLN, mantida pela Explosion.ai. Lançada em 2016, suporta 73 idiomas e é focada em uso em produção, com modelos pré-treinados de diferentes tamanhos.
coverage_criteria: Identificar o spaCy como biblioteca de PLN com foco em produção.
Diferenciar spaCy de outras bibliotecas como NLTK (acadêmico).
Citar que suporta múltiplos idiomas e oferece modelos pequenos, médios e grandes.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

anchors.locator: Instalação e uso básico do spaCy

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo apresenta o spaCy, sua origem, licença, mantenedores e diferenciais em relação a outras bibliotecas.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: É necessário que o aluno saiba o que é o spaCy e suas características antes de usar a biblioteca.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Modelos spaCy: blank vs pré-treinados e tamanhos
before_phase4_candidates.description: O spaCy permite criar modelos em branco (blank) com regras específicas de um idioma, ou carregar modelos pré-treinados (sm, md, lg) que já vêm com pesos estatísticos. Modelos maiores oferecem mais acurácia, mas são mais lentos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar a diferença entre blank('pt') e load('pt_core_news_lg').
Dizer que modelos pré-treinados incluem pesos para tarefas como POS e NER.
Comparar trade-offs de tamanho (pequeno, médio, grande) em velocidade e acurácia.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo mostra a diferença entre blank e pré-treinado, e discute os tamanhos (12MB, 40MB, 541MB) e a relação eficiência vs acurácia.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: O conceito é básico para iniciar o uso do spaCy e escolher o modelo adequado para uma tarefa.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Tokenização – como o spaCy divide o texto em unidades
before_phase4_candidates.description: Tokenização é o processo de dividir um texto em unidades linguísticas chamadas tokens (palavras, pontuação, etc.). Cada língua tem seu próprio tokenizador. Tokens são a base para análises como POS e dependências.
coverage_criteria: Definir tokenização e dar exemplos de tokens (palavras, pontos).
Explicar que o tokenizador depende do idioma.
Usar list(doc) para visualizar os tokens de uma frase.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

anchors.locator: Tokenização: Base para entender o contexto

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo destaca a tokenização como a primeira etapa essencial, mostrando como o spaCy separa 'Eduardo foi à feira.' em tokens e discute regras específicas do português.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: É um conceito fundamental e isolável; pode ser verificado com uma simples pergunta sobre o resultado de tokenizar uma frase.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Contêineres spaCy: Doc, Token e Span
before_phase4_candidates.description: No spaCy, um Doc representa o documento inteiro processado, contendo uma sequência de objetos Token. Um Span é uma fatia de um Doc (um agrupamento de tokens consecutivos). Esses contêineres são a base para navegar e acessar atributos linguísticos.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é um Doc e como criá-lo via nlp(texto).
Descrever Token como uma unidade individual com atributos.
Demonstrar como criar um Span usando slicing (doc[0:3]).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo dedica uma seção aos 'containers básicos', ilustrando com diagrama e código as relações entre Doc, Token e Span.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Esses três tipos são os alicerces para toda manipulação no spaCy; o aluno precisa saber diferenciá-los e usá-los.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Atributos de tokens no spaCy: text, shape_ e is_alpha
before_phase4_candidates.description: Cada token possui atributos que descrevem sua forma e tipo: `.text` retorna o texto original; `.shape_` descreve a forma (maiúsculas/minúsculas, dígitos); `.is_alpha` indica se é alfabético. Esses atributos permitem filtrar ou identificar padrões no texto.
coverage_criteria: Listar e definir os atributos text, shape_ e is_alpha.
Fornecer um exemplo de uso de shape_ para identificar números ('589' -> 'DDD').
Usar is_alpha para separar palavras de pontuação ou números.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

anchors.locator: Atributos dos Tokens: Text, Shape, Is_alpha

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo mostra uma seção específica sobre esses atributos, com exemplos em código e explicação de por que shapes como 'DDD' são úteis para machine learning.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Atributos básicos dos tokens são uma habilidade prática imediata; verifica-se com um pequeno código.

before_phase4_candidates.label: POS tagging – classificação gramatical dos tokens
before_phase4_candidates.description: POS tagging atribui a cada token uma classe gramatical (e.g., substantivo, verbo, adjetivo) segundo o esquema Universal Dependencies. No spaCy, o atributo `.pos_` retorna o tag (e.g., NOUN, VERB, ADJ) e `.tag_` fornece detalhes mais granulares.
coverage_criteria: Explicar que POS tagging identifica a função gramatical de cada token.
Usar .pos_ para obter tags como PROPN, VERB, NOUN.
Dar um exemplo com uma frase simples e listar as tags obtidas.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

anchors.locator: Isso no código: Atributos léxicos em tabela

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo dedica uma seção à análise sintática e mostra como obter as tags POS, incluindo exemplos com 'Eduardo' (PROPN) e 'faz' (VERB).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: POS é uma das análises linguísticas mais comuns; um aluno deve saber extraí-la e interpretá-la.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Lematização – redução de palavras à sua forma canônica
before_phase4_candidates.description: Lematização transforma palavras flexionadas (plural, conjugações) em sua forma base ou lema. Ex.: 'faz' -> 'fazer', 'gatos' -> 'gato'. No spaCy, acessa-se via `.lemma_`. É diferente de stemming, que corta radicais.
coverage_criteria: Definir lematização e diferenciar de stemming.
Mostrar como obter o lema de um token com .lemma_.
Dar um exemplo: 'comprou' -> 'comprar'.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

anchors.locator: Isso no código: Atributos léxicos em tabela

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: O vídeo explica a lematização como desflexionar palavras, usando exemplos como 'faz' -> 'fazer' e 'gatos' -> 'gato'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: É uma técnica essencial para normalização de texto; pode ser verificada com uma pergunta direta.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Análise de dependências sintáticas (dep_)
before_phase4_candidates.description: A análise de dependências atribui a cada token um rótulo `.dep_` que indica sua relação sintática com o núcleo da frase (ex.: nsubj para sujeito nominal, obj para objeto). Permite entender a estrutura da frase.
coverage_criteria: Explicar que dep_ mostra a função sintática (sujeito, objeto).
Identificar o nsubj de um verbo em uma frase.
Usar displacy.render para visualizar as dependências.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Reconhecimento de Entidades Nomeadas (NER) no spaCy
before_phase4_candidates.description: NER identifica entidades como pessoas, organizações, locais, etc., dentro do texto. No spaCy, acessível via `doc.ents` e atributos `.label_` dos tokens. Suporta diversos tipos como PERSON, ORG, GPE, MISC.
coverage_criteria: Definir NER e listar exemplos (PERSON, ORG).
Extrair entidades de um texto usando doc.ents.
Imprimir o texto e o label de cada entidade.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: (Vídeo) spaCy: Introdução a Processamento de Linguagem Natural

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Conceito isolável e verificável com exemplo prático de extração de entidades de uma frase.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Default Copyright on Unlicensed Repositories
before_phase4_candidates.description: If a public repository does not include a license, default copyright laws apply, meaning only the original author holds rights to reproduce, distribute, or create derivative works.
coverage_criteria: Explain the implications of not having a license file in a public repository.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source states that without a license, 'as leis padrão de copyright' apply, denying others the right to use, alter, or distribute the software.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept that can be checked with a single question about default copyright.

before_phase4_candidates.label: ChooseaLicense.com as a Decision Tool
before_phase4_candidates.description: GitHub provides choosealicense.com to help developers select an appropriate open source license by understanding the permissions and restrictions of each license.
coverage_criteria: Describe the purpose of choosealicense.com and how it helps with license selection.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article introduces choosealicense.com as a resource created to assist in understanding licensing.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific tool mention that can be quizzed with a question about its function.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Conventional License File Location and Naming
before_phase4_candidates.description: Most projects place the license text in a file named LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md, or LICENSE.rst in the repository root. Some projects include license information in the README instead.
coverage_criteria: State the conventional file name and location for a license in a repository, and mention an alternative location.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly describes the common practice of placing LICENSE.txt in the root and gives an example, also noting that some use README.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific, checkable convention that can be answered in a single sentence.

before_phase4_candidates.label: GitHub Terms of Service on Public Repositories
before_phase4_candidates.description: According to GitHub's Terms of Service, publishing code in a public repository grants other users the right to view and fork the repository, even without a license.
coverage_criteria: Explain what rights other GitHub users have over a public repository without a license according to GitHub TOS.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article notes that despite lack of license, GitHub TOS allows viewing and forking, serving as a warning.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a distinct legal nuance that can be checked with a targeted question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Filtering Repositories by License on GitHub
before_phase4_candidates.description: GitHub search supports the `license:` qualifier with a specific license keyword to filter repositories by their license type.
coverage_criteria: Demonstrate how to search for repositories using a specific license, e.g., `license:MIT`.

anchors.locator: Pesquisando GitHub por tipo de licença

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides a table of license keywords and explains using the `license:` qualifier for search.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical skill that can be tested by asking to construct a search query.

before_phase4_candidates.label: License Family Search

anchors.locator: Pesquisando GitHub por tipo de licença

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific feature of GitHub search that can be assessed with a scenario-based question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Automated License Detection using Licensee
before_phase4_candidates.description: The open-source tool Licensee compares a repository's LICENSE file against a short list of known licenses to automatically identify the license used.
coverage_criteria: Explain what Licensee does and how it helps identify project licenses.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces Licensee, describes its function, and notes its use by GitHub.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a named tool and a distinct concept about license identification that can be explained concisely.

before_phase4_candidates.label: License Picker During Repository Creation
before_phase4_candidates.description: When creating a new repository on GitHub, a license picker dropdown allows you to select and add a license template automatically.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Manual License Addition via Browser

anchors.locator: Aplicar uma licença em um repositório com uma licença existente

before_phase4_candidates.label: Existing Forks Survive Visibility Change
before_phase4_candidates.description: If you change a public repository to private, any forks or local copies created while it was public will continue to exist.
coverage_criteria: Explain what happens to existing forks when a repository is made private.

reconciled_candidates.label: Exploring pre-loaded Portuguese texts with NLTK
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can load Portuguese example texts from NLTK's examples module and use methods like concordance, similar, collocations, findall (with regex), and generate to explore text properties and patterns.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load Portuguese text objects from nltk.examples and list their descriptions.
Use concordance() to display a word in context, and similar() to find words with similar distribution.
Extract significant collocations using collocations() and use findall() with a regex to find pattern matches.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates teach essential exploration methods available for pre-loaded Portuguese texts in NLTK, forming a coherent unit of text discovery techniques.

reconciled_candidates.label: Basic text processing as lists of words in NLTK
reconciled_candidates.description: Students understand that tokenized text is a list of tokens, and can extract unique vocabulary using set/sorted, transform tokens with list comprehensions, and compute frequency distributions with FreqDist.
coverage_criteria: Explain that a tokenized sentence is a list of string tokens and inspect its length.
Write code to obtain the sorted unique vocabulary from a tokenized list.
Use a list comprehension to filter or transform tokens, and create a FreqDist to find the most common word.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover fundamental text processing operations that treat text as a list of tokens, essential for any NLTK-based analysis.

reconciled_candidates.label: Accessing specialized Portuguese corpora in NLTK
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can load and explore the Machado de Assis corpus, MacMorpho POS-tagged corpus, and Floresta treebank, including accessing words, tagged words, parsed sentences, and extracting n-grams containing a target word.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load the Machado corpus, list file IDs, and access the words of a specific work.
Demonstrate loading MacMorpho and distinguishing between simple words and tagged tokens.
Retrieve parsed sentences from Floresta and simplify a complex POS tag.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates involve accessing and utilizing different Portuguese-specific NLTK corpora, providing a comprehensive overview of available linguistic resources.

reconciled_candidates.label: Practical skills: text encoding and concordance implementation
reconciled_candidates.description: Students understand the need for ISO 8859-1 encoding when working with Portuguese text in NLTK and can implement a basic concordance function from scratch.
coverage_criteria: Explain why ISO 8859-1 encoding is used for Portuguese text in NLTK and how to decode such text.
Write a function that implements a simple concordance for a given word and context window.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover practical, hands-on skills that complement the main text processing pipeline, ensuring students can handle real-world text data.

reconciled_candidates.label: Tokenization using NLTK's word_tokenize
reconciled_candidates.description: Students learn to use nltk.word_tokenize for accurate tokenization that properly handles English contractions like 'wasn't' into 'was' and "n't".
coverage_criteria: Explain why nltk.word_tokenize is better than a simple regex split for handling contractions.
Apply nltk.word_tokenize to a sentence with contractions and explain the resulting tokens.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a distinct technique for improved tokenization in NLTK.

reconciled_candidates.label: Stemming with NLTK (Porter and Snowball)
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can apply Porter Stemmer and Snowball Stemmer to reduce words to their stems, and understand the differences between rule-based and multilingual stemming.
coverage_criteria: Use PorterStemmer to stem a list of words and note that stems may not be real words.
Initialize SnowballStemmer for a specific language and compare its output on 'generously' to Porter Stemmer.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates teach stemming algorithms, covering the classic Porter and the multilingual Snowball, which together provide a solid understanding of stemming in NLTK.

reconciled_candidates.label: Lemmatization with NLTK WordNet
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can use WordNetLemmatizer to obtain dictionary base forms of words, understanding the difference between lemmatization and stemming.
coverage_criteria: Explain the difference between lemmatization and stemming.
Instantiate WordNetLemmatizer and lemmatize a plural noun or a verb to its lemma.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as the primary lemmatization method in NLTK, distinct from stemming.

reconciled_candidates.label: spaCy fundamentals: pipelines and data structures
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can create a blank language pipeline, process text into a Doc object, and access Tokens and Spans within it.
coverage_criteria: Write code to create a blank Portuguese pipeline and process 'Olá mundo' to get a Doc.
Retrieve a specific token and create a Span from a Doc.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover the core spaCy workflow: initializing a pipeline and understanding its output data structures.

reconciled_candidates.label: Pattern detection with spaCy lexical attributes
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can use token attributes like `like_num` to detect patterns in a text, such as identifying percentages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to find numeric tokens in a Doc using `like_num`.
Write a loop to detect a number followed by a '%' sign.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a specific technique for pattern detection, leveraging spaCy's built-in lexical attributes.

reconciled_candidates.label: Loading and understanding trained spaCy pipelines
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can load pre-trained pipelines like pt_core_news_sm, and understand that pipeline packages contain configuration, weights, and vocabulary but not training data.
coverage_criteria: Load the Portuguese small pipeline and process a simple text.
List the components included in a trained pipeline package and explain why training data is absent.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates together teach loading pre-trained spaCy models and understanding their contents, essential for using advanced NLP features.

reconciled_candidates.label: Predicting linguistic annotations with spaCy
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can access part-of-speech tags, dependency labels, and named entities from a Doc processed with a trained spaCy pipeline.
coverage_criteria: Write a loop to print each token's text, .pos_, and .dep_ after processing with a Portuguese pipeline.
Iterate over doc.ents and print entity text and label, using spacy.explain to describe a label.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates cover predicting and extracting linguistic annotations—POS, dependencies, and named entities—which are standard outputs of a trained spaCy pipeline.

reconciled_candidates.label: Manually correcting spaCy entity predictions
reconciled_candidates.description: Students can manually create a Span to represent an entity that a trained model failed to recognize, demonstrating awareness of model limitations.
coverage_criteria: Given a Doc where an entity is missed, write code to create a Span for the relevant tokens.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate stands alone as a practical skill for handling imperfect model predictions, emphasizing manual intervention.

reconciled_candidates.label: Rule-based pattern matching with spaCy Matcher
reconciled_candidates.description: How to use spaCy's Matcher class to find token sequences based on patterns, from simple literal matches to complex patterns using token attributes, lemmas, POS tags, and quantifiers.
coverage_criteria: Initialize a Matcher, add a pattern, apply it to a Doc, and retrieve matches.
Write patterns that use lemmas, POS tags, and quantifiers (+, *, ?) to match flexible sequences.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates cover the Matcher; 009 introduces basic usage, 010 extends to complex patterns. Together they form the complete teachable concept of rule-based matching.

reconciled_candidates.label: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
reconciled_candidates.description: NLP is the field that studies how to make computers understand natural language, relying on statistical approximations due to the non-computable nature of language, leading to uncertainties and false positives.
coverage_criteria: Explain that NLP deals with machine understanding of natural language.
Mention that approaches are statistical and approximate.
Give examples of applications like information extraction or chatbots.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate that introduces the foundational NLP concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: spaCy: a production-ready NLP library
reconciled_candidates.description: spaCy is an open-source (MIT) NLP library maintained by Explosion.ai, designed for production use, supporting 73 languages and offering various pre-trained models. It contrasts with academic-focused libraries like NLTK.
coverage_criteria: Identify spaCy as a production-oriented NLP library.
Name its maintainer and license.
State that it supports multiple languages and offers small, medium, and large models.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate that introduces the spaCy library.

reconciled_candidates.label: spaCy model types: blank vs pre-trained and size trade-offs
reconciled_candidates.description: spaCy allows creating blank models with language-specific rules, or loading pre-trained models (sm, md, lg) that include statistical weights for tasks like POS and NER. Larger models are more accurate but slower.
coverage_criteria: Explain the difference between blank('pt') and load('pt_core_news_lg').
State that pre-trained models contain weights for NLP tasks.
Compare the trade-offs of model sizes in speed and accuracy.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate that teaches model selection in spaCy.

reconciled_candidates.label: Tokenization and core data structures in spaCy (Doc, Token, Span)
reconciled_candidates.description: Tokenization splits text into linguistic units (tokens) using language-specific tokenizers. The resulting Doc holds Token objects, and Span slices represent contiguous token groups. These are the foundation for navigating processed text.
coverage_criteria: Define tokenization and give examples of tokens.
Explain that tokenizers are language-specific.
Create a Doc, access tokens via iteration, and use slicing to obtain a Span.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Tokenization (004) and the container types (005) are inseparable; together they teach the essential data flow in spaCy.

reconciled_candidates.label: Accessing token attributes: text, shape_, is_alpha
reconciled_candidates.description: Tokens expose attributes describing their form: .text returns the original string, .shape_ shows the character pattern (e.g., 'DDD' for digits), and .is_alpha checks if the token is alphabetic. These are useful for filtering and pattern detection.
coverage_criteria: Retrieve token.text, token.shape_, and token.is_alpha.
Use shape_ to identify tokens like numbers and dates.
Use is_alpha to separate words from punctuation or numbers.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate covering basic non-linguistic token inspection.

reconciled_candidates.label: Part-of-speech tagging in spaCy
reconciled_candidates.description: POS tagging assigns each token a grammatical class (e.g., NOUN, VERB) using the Universal Dependencies schema, accessed via .pos_. The .tag_ attribute provides finer-grained tags.
coverage_criteria: Explain that POS tagging identifies the function of a token.
Use token.pos_ to retrieve tags like PROPN, VERB, NOUN.
Print POS tags for a simple sentence.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate for a key linguistic annotation step.

reconciled_candidates.label: Lemmatization in spaCy
reconciled_candidates.description: Lemmatization reduces inflected words to their base dictionary form (e.g., 'faz' → 'fazer') using token.lemma_. It differs from stemming, which simply chops suffixes.
coverage_criteria: Define lemmatization and contrast with stemming.
Obtain the lemma of a token with token.lemma_.
Demonstrate with an example like 'comprou' → 'comprar'.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate that teaches a normalization technique.

reconciled_candidates.label: Dependency parsing in spaCy
reconciled_candidates.description: Dependency parsing labels each token with its syntactic role (e.g., nsubj, obj) via token.dep_, showing how words relate to the sentence head. The displacy.render function visualizes these relations.
coverage_criteria: Explain that dep_ indicates syntactic function like subject or object.
Find the nsubj of a verb in a sentence.
Use displacy.render to visualize dependencies.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate for syntactic analysis.

reconciled_candidates.label: Named Entity Recognition (NER) in spaCy
reconciled_candidates.description: NER identifies entities such as persons (PERSON), organizations (ORG), and locations in text. Access entity spans via doc.ents and their labels with .label_.
coverage_criteria: Define NER and give examples like PERSON, ORG.
Extract entities from a text using doc.ents.
Print the text and label of each entity.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate for entity extraction.

reconciled_candidates.label: Legal defaults for repositories without a license: copyright and GitHub Terms of Service
reconciled_candidates.description: When a public repository has no license, default copyright law applies, and GitHub's ToS allow viewing and forking. This teaches the implications of omitting a license.
coverage_criteria: Explain how default copyright restricts usage of an unlicensed repo.
State what GitHub ToS permit for public repositories without a license.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates address consequences of missing licenses; combined they form a single cautionary concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Choosing an open-source license using choosealicense.com
reconciled_candidates.description: choosealicense.com helps developers select an appropriate open-source license by explaining permissions and restrictions, making the decision easier.
coverage_criteria: Describe the purpose of choosealicense.com.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate focused on the license selection tool.

reconciled_candidates.label: Adding a license to a GitHub repository: conventions and methods
reconciled_candidates.description: Standard practices for placing a license file include naming it LICENSE.txt and putting it in the repository root. GitHub offers a license picker when creating a repo, and you can manually add a file via the web interface.
coverage_criteria: State the conventional file name and location for a license.
Describe the GitHub license picker feature during repo creation.
Outline the steps to manually add a license file using GitHub's web interface.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover the procedural aspects of adding a license file; together they form a single teachable concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Searching and identifying open-source licenses on GitHub
reconciled_candidates.description: GitHub search supports the license: qualifier with specific keywords or license family names (e.g., GPL). The Licensee tool automatically detects a repository’s license by comparing its LICENSE file against known licenses.
coverage_criteria: Construct a search query using license:MIT.
Explain the result of searching license:gpl.
Describe what Licensee does to identify a project's license.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All three cover aspects of finding or detecting licenses; combined they teach the complete skill of license discovery on GitHub.

reconciled_candidates.label: Important caveats about GitHub licensing information
reconciled_candidates.description: GitHub’s licensing guidance is provided ‘as-is’ and is not legal advice. Existing forks of a public repository persist even if the repository is later made private.
coverage_criteria: Recall that GitHub's license content is not legal advice.
Explain what happens to forks when a repository is made private.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both are disclaimers/exceptions related to licensing; they form a single cautionary concept.
